headline: High-risk shared filesystem and broad egress create prompt-injection, leakage, and cascading-action exposure between Cursor and emqx.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Cursor can read/write workspace files, open buffers, clipboard, and use MCP; its shared_state_with_other_instances is via local filesystem. emqx exposes HTTP API and broad network egress. That creates a plausible bridge where attacker-controlled content from one side can be consumed by the other, though no direct parser bridge is documented, so I choose medium over low.
conditions: IF Cursor reads content from a shared workspace file that emqx can influence, prompt injection is possible.
IF emqx ingests text originating from Cursor without provenance checks, instruction hijacking is possible.
mitigations: Separate workspaces and disable shared local filesystem exchange.
Require provenance tags on any file or message passed between agents.
Disable MCP endpoints not needed for the task.
Review and sanitize any text before feeding it into either agent.
requires-engineering: add content-origin filtering in the orchestrator.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Cursor touches source code, open files, and clipboard contents, and can write/read the filesystem. emqx touches IoT data and has broad network egress plus an HTTP API. A shared workspace or copied content could leak sensitive material from Cursor into emqx outputs or network traffic; the profiles do not prove a default leak, but the pathway exists.
conditions: IF both agents access the same local workspace, sensitive files can flow from Cursor to emqx.
IF Cursor clipboard contents are pasted into emqx-facing inputs, clipboard data may be exposed.
mitigations: Use separate OS users or containers for each agent.
Keep sensitive files out of any shared directory.
Disable clipboard-based transfer between agents.
Restrict emqx egress to approved destinations.
requires-engineering: add DLP/redaction before any cross-agent handoff.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Cursor has unrestricted filesystem write, modify_git_state, shell, and broad egress; its shared state is via local filesystem. emqx has broad network egress and an HTTP API. If both operate on the same mutable workspace or repo, concurrent writes and git-state changes can collide and corrupt state. The overlap is directly supported by both profiles, so high is warranted.
conditions: IF both agents write to the same directory, file clobbering can occur.
IF Cursor modifies git state while emqx writes artifacts into the repo, repository corruption or lost updates can occur.
mitigations: Assign disjoint directories to each agent.
Pause one agent while the other performs writes.
Use git locks or a single-writer policy.
Snapshot the workspace before concurrent runs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking for shared mutable resources.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Cursor can generate code, files, and agent outputs; emqx exposes an HTTP API and broad egress, so downstream automation could consume Cursor output as authoritative. The profiles do not show explicit verification between them, making a mistaken output-to-action chain plausible. Because the action authority is indirect rather than explicit, medium fits.
conditions: IF emqx consumes Cursor-produced text or config without validation, errors can cascade into downstream actions.
IF Cursor emits malformed instructions that emqx forwards via HTTP API, the mistake propagates.
mitigations: Insert a human review step before any actioning.
Validate schemas on all Cursor-to-emqx handoffs.
Require emqx to reject unsigned or unverified inputs.
Log and diff handoffs before execution.
requires-engineering: implement typed contracts between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Cursor is closed-source and handles source code, open files, clipboard contents, and model-provider APIs; emqx is open-source and touches IoT data with HTTP API exposure. The profiles do not show a concrete residency or certification mismatch, so only a low compliance concern is supported. I do not cite only one agent because the risk is about the pair's combined data flow.
conditions: IF regulated IoT data from emqx is routed into Cursor's cloud-backed model providers, policy review is needed.
IF source code or clipboard data from Cursor is retained alongside IoT data in emqx logs, retention mismatch may arise.
mitigations: Review data retention settings in both tools.
Avoid sending regulated data into Cursor prompts.
Minimize logging on emqx-facing inputs.
Document the data flow for compliance review.
requires-engineering: align residency and retention controls across both systems.
